Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Julian had been thirty when the stalking began, a quiet erosion of his daily rhythm that eventually altered it. It started with a neighbor’s persistent attention, a man who began leaving unmarked envelopes, then lingering in the driveway. The turning point came in late October when a motorcycle idled outside Julian’s house for nearly four hours. He watched from the kitchen window as the rider adjusted his helmet, the engine’s low rumble vibrating through the floorboards. When Julian stepped onto the porch to ask for privacy, the rider’s calm, polite expression tightened into something sharp and unyielding. That calm-to-anger shift lodged itself in Julian. He had come to believe that quietness was merely the pause before the storm, and that anger, however measured, was never truly harmless. In the months that followed, Julian’s world narrowed. He found himself unable to settle into sleep, his mind replaying the sensation of being watched, his body braced for a sound that might mean the motorcycle was back. He began avoiding unfamiliar places, pacing the aisles of grocery stores and parking lots, constantly scanning the periphery. What frightened him most was the false alarm; a car door would slam down the street, and Julian would step outside, heart hammering, convinced the rider had returned, even though the street was empty. Over time, these reactions settled into routine. Punishment thinking coexisted with his growing tendency to pull back from his wife, Clara. He avoided intimacy, finding it difficult to let her rest her head on his chest or speak freely, certain that people were not what they seemed, and that, fundamentally, they could not be trusted. He avoided relaxation, finding that stillness felt dangerous, and carried this posture through his days. His inability to trust that he would do the right thing surfaced clearly in his work. He would second-guess his explanations, rewrite notes, and rehearse questions, certain that a wrong turn might invite the same relentless attention that had once cornered him. His work as a tutor provided the concrete stage where these patterns played out. Julian conducted sessions in the sunlit room of his suburban home, where large windows looked out onto the street. When he taught a particularly talkative high school student, the boy’s sudden sigh or the soft click of the radiator would make Julian’s breath catch. He would pause his lesson, glancing toward the driveway, assessing whether the noise was merely domestic or a sign of being tracked. The motor rumble from the street below sometimes echoed the old rider’s approach, and Julian would feel his shoulders rise, caught between the present lesson and the lingering sensation of being followed. Punishment thinking settled alongside these moments; he told himself he deserved this constant vigilance, that the discomfort was his due. None of these patterns drove the others. They simply occupied the same space, layering over his marriage, his home, and his tutoring practice. Now, at thirty-two, Julian sits in a quiet therapist’s office, the familiar hum of the building masking the distant city sounds. His clinical questionnaire score sat at fifty-nine, a number that mirrored the weight he carried each day. He came because the accumulation of his habits has begun to press heavily on his marriage and his students, and because he is tired of living in a state of suspended warning. He does not expect the fear to vanish entirely, but he is hoping for a place where he can lower his guard without danger following him in. What he fears most, he tells the therapist, is the quiet moments—the unannounced glances, the unexplained sounds—because he is certain that people can slip past his defenses at any time, and that he will be left to bear the weight of it alone.
